                                             Noise sensitivity of percolation via differential inequalities
                                                                  Vincent Tassion∗             Hugo Vanneuville∗



                                                                                      Abstract
                                                     Consider critical Bernoulli percolation in the plane. We give a new proof of the




arXiv:2011.04572v2 [math.PR] 18 Jan 2023
                                                 sharp noise sensitivity theorem shown by Garban, Pete and Schramm in [GPS10].
                                                 Contrary to the previous approaches, we do not use any spectral tool. We rather
                                                 study differential inequalities satisfied by a dynamical four-arm event, in the spirit
                                                 of Kesten’s proof of scaling relations in [Kes87]. We also obtain new results in
                                                 dynamical percolation. In particular, we prove that the Hausdorff dimension of the
                                                 set of times with both primal and dual percolation equals 2/3 a.s.


                                                 Contents
                                                 1 Introduction                                                                      2

                                                 2 Discussion and sketch of proof                                                    8

                                                 3 A dynamical Margulis–Russo formula                                               11

                                                 4 Quasi-multiplicativity for dynamical arm events                                  14

                                                 5 Differential inequalities                                                        15

                                                 6 Superquadratic decay above the sensitivity length                                20

                                                 7 Sharp noise sensitivity for arm events                                           23

                                                 8 Sharp noise sensitivity for crossing events                                      24

                                                 9 Applications to dynamical percolation                                            26

                                                 10 Bond percolation on Z2                                                          27

1     Introduction
1.1    Noise sensitivity of percolation
Given some integer n ≥ 1, we consider the discrete hypercube {0, 1}n endowed with
the uniform probability measure
                                                    ⊗n
                                           δ1 + δ0
                                  P=
                                              2

and we let E be the corresponding expectation. Let t ∈ [0, 1], let X ∼ P, and
let Y ∼ P be obtained from X by resampling independently each coordinate with
probability t. A function f from {0, 1}n to {0, 1} is called a Boolean function, and
we study the covariance

               COVt (f ) = Cov(f (X), f (Y )) = E[f (X)f (Y )] − E[f ]2 .

(As usually, P and E refer to the underlying probability measure and expectation
under which X and Y are defined, hence our use of the two different notations (E, P)
and (E, P).)
    It is well known that COVt (f ) is non-increasing in t (see for instance Proposi-
tion 3.1), and in this paper we are interested in the following question: For which
values of t does the quantity COVt (f ) get small? Or, in words, when do f (X)
and f (Y ) start to become “roughly independent”? Noise sensitivity, in the sense of
[BKS99], corresponds to the asymptotic version of this question.
    In the present study, it will be convenient to introduce the quadratic form Qt ,
defined by
                                Qt (f ) = E[f (X)f (Y )]
for every f : {0, 1}n → {0, 1}, and Qt (A) = Qt (1A ) for every event A ⊆ {0, 1}n .
With this notation, the covariance introduced above can be rewritten as COVt (f ) =
Qt (f ) − Q1 (f ).
    In the present work, we consider Boolean functions in the context of critical
face percolation on the (regular) hexagonal lattice (which is the same as critical site
percolation on the triangular lattice). Although all planar percolation models “with
enough symmetries” are believed to behave the same (asymptotically), much more
is known about this model, due to the proof of conformal invariance by Smirnov
[Smi01]. By using this property, the SLE processes introduced by Schramm, and
Kesten’s proof of scaling relations [Kes87], Lawler, Schramm and Werner [LSW02]
and Smirnov and Werner [SW01] have computed several critical exponents (see Sec-
tion 9.1). This will be crucial in Sections 1.3 and 9. However, outside of these
sections, we will only use results that are known both for face percolation on the
hexagonal lattice and bond percolation on the square lattice, for which conformal
invariance has not been proven. In Section 10, we state explicitly the results that
we prove for bond percolation on Z2 .
    Let us define face percolation on the hexagonal lattice. Let H be the set of faces
of this lattice. An element ω ∈ {0, 1}H induces a coloring of the plane as follows: the
hexagon H ∈ H is colored in black (resp. white) if ωH = 1 (resp. ωH = 0). Given a
parameter p ∈ [0, 1], we equip the space {0, 1}H with the product σ-algebra and the
product probability measure (pδ1 + (1 − p)δ0 )⊗H . Kesten has proven in [Kes80] that


                                            2
the critical parameter of this model is pc = 1/2. More precisely, if p ≤ 1/2 then a.s.
there is no unbounded black component while this is a.s. the case if p > 1/2. We
refer to [Gri99, BR06, Wer07, GS14] for more about planar Bernoulli percolation.
    For every integer n ≥ 1, let Hn be the set of hexagons that intersect the square
[0, n]2 and let gn : {0, 1}Hn → {0, 1} denote the indicator function of the left-right
crossing of [0, n]2 , that is, the event that there is a continuous black path included in
[0, n]2 that connects the left side of this square and its right side. Since pc = 1/2, the
measure induced on the hypercube {0, 1}Hn by critical percolation is the uniform
probability measure P already considered above.
    In [BKS99], Benjamini, Kalai and Schramm have introduced the notion of noise
sensitivity and have proven that the crossing events are noise sensitive, that is,

                               ∀t ∈ (0, 1]    COVt (gn ) −→ 0.
                                                                 n→+∞

In [SS10], Schramm and Steif have proven the following quantitative noise sensitivity
result: There exists c > 0 such that COVtn (gn ) → 0 for any sequence (tn )n≥1 that
satisfies tn ≥ n−c . The sharp noise sensitivity theorem has then been proven by
Garban, Pete and Schramm in [GPS10]. In order to state this result, let us denote
by αn the probability that there exist four arms of alternating colors from scale 1
to scale n (see the beginning of Section 1.2 for a more precise definition) and let
                                                        1
                                             εn =            .
                                                    n2 αn
(See the next subsection and the sketch of proof – in Section 2.1 – for some intuition
behind the importance of the four-arm event in the study of noise sensitivity.)
                                                                                   ∗
Theorem 1.1 (Sharp noise sensitivity, [GPS10]). Let (tn )n≥1 ∈ [0, 1]N and let gn
be the indicator of the left-right crossing of [0, n]2 . We have
                          tn
                   lim         = +∞          =⇒             lim COVtn (gn ) = 0,
                 n→+∞ εn                                 n→+∞

and
                           tn                                               1
                    lim          =0      =⇒             lim COVtn (gn ) =     .
                   n→+∞ εn                              n→+∞                4
   For face percolation on the triangular lattice, it has been proven in [SW01]
that αn = n−5/4+o(1) , thus εn = n−3/4+o(1) . Except when computing Hausdorff
dimensions of exceptional times for dynamical percolation (see Section 1.3), we will
not need the exact values of these exponents, and we will mostly rely on the following
lower bound on the ratio αn /αm (which is known both for face percolation on H and
bond percolation on Z2 , see for instance [GS14, Lemma 6.5]): There exists c > 0
such that, for every n ≥ m ≥ 1,
                                      αn     m 2−c
                                         ≥c          .                                 (1)
                                      αm      n
   The proofs from [BKS99, SS10, GPS10] rely on the study of the Fourier spectrum
of Boolean functions. Spectral tools are very rich (they are for instance connected
to the theories of influences, hypercontractivity, decision trees etc. – see [GS14,
O’D14]), but some limitations appear when dealing with non-monotonic events (see


                                                    3
       Open Problem 8 of [GPS10])1 , and more importantly, the Fourier analysis have not
       been developed for other models of statistical mechanics, such as FK-percolation.
       In the present work, we give a new proof of Theorem 1.1 without relying on any
       spectral tool. We also obtain new results for noise sensitivity of non-monotonic
       events, and we hope that this approach can be used to tackle noise sensitivity results
       for Markov dynamics associated to non product measure. The main object of our
       proof is the dynamical four-arm event introduced in Section 1.2, that we study via
       a strategy inspired by Kesten’s work on near-critical percolation [Kes87] (see also
       [Wer07, Nol08]).
       Remark 1.2. In Section 8, we will actually compute COVt (gn ) up to constant
       factors (see Equation (32)). This quantitative version of Theorem 1.1 is equivalent
       to the main spectral estimate from [GPS10], that is, Theorem 1.1 therein. Let us
       note that, on the contrary, the geometric spectral results from [GPS10] (for instance
       the partial spatial independence and clustering properties, see also [GV19, GHSS21])
       cannot be extracted from such a non-spectral result.
           We refer to [BGS13, For16] for the study of noise sensitivity for another type of
       noise, namely the exclusion noise. Noise sensitivity has also been studied for other
       planar percolation models (that are believed to behave similarly to Bernoulli per-
       colation): Poisson Boolean percolation [ABGM14], Voronoi percolation [AGMT16,
       AB18] and percolation of nodal lines [GV20]. This notion has also been studied for
       Erdős–Renyi percolation [LS15, RŞ18, LP20] and bootstrap percolation [BP15]. See
       the books [GS14, O’D14] for more about noise sensitivity and Boolean functions.

       1.2     Arm events
       If n ≥ m ≥ 1, we let Hm,n denote the set of hexagons that intersect the annulus
       [−n, n]2 \ (−m, m)2 and we call an arm of type 1 (resp. type 0) from m to n a
       continuous black (resp. white) path from ∂[−m, m]2 to ∂[−n, n]2 included in the
       annulus [−n, n]2 \ (−m, m)2 . For j ≥ 1, σ ∈ {0, 1}j and n ≥ m ≥ j, define
                                        σ
                                       fm,n : {0, 1}Hm,n → {0, 1}

       to be the indicator of the event that there exist j disjoint2 arms from m to n with
       respective types σ1 , . . . , σj , in the counter-clockwise order. Such an event is called
       an arm event. See Figure 1 for an illustration of the alternating four-arm event.
                                                                      σ
           Note that the assumption n ≥ m ≥ j implies that E[fm,n         ] > 0. If 1 ≤ m ≤ n < j
                                                     σ                                  σ     σ
       or 1 ≤ n < m, we use the convention fm,n ≡ 1; if 1 ≤ m < j ≤ n, we let fm,n         = fj,n .
       Define also

       the additional constraint that the arms stay in the (upper) half-plane, and the arm
       types are from right to left. Given an arm type ? (i.e. ? = σ or σ+), we define
                                     ?        ?

     and for every t ∈ [0, 1]

                                πm,n (t) = Qt (fm,n ),     πn? (t) = Qt (fn? ).
                                                             ?
     Since we will often see t as a time parameter, we call πm,n (t) a dynamical arm event
     probability. Note that we have the following “boundary conditions”:
                                 ?          ?         ?           ?
                                πm,n (0) = αm,n ,    πm,n (1) = (αm,n )2 .
     The study of the (alternating) four-arm event, which corresponds to the arm type
     ? = 0101, is at the core of our proof. This event corresponds to the geometric
     interpretation of pivotality for crossing events (see the beginning of Section 3 for the
     definition of pivotality). When considering this event, we will omit the exponent in
     our notation and simply write
                                            0101                 0101
                                    αm,n = αm,n  ,       πm,n = πm,n  .
     (And similarly for αn and πn .) One can note that πn (t) is the probability that the
     origin has a four-arm both at times 0 and t.
        For each t ∈ (0, 1], we let
                                  `(t) = min{n ≥ 1 : n2 αn ≥ 1/t}.                       (2)
     By (1) with m = 1, n2 αn → +∞. As a result, `(t) is a well defined positive integer
     that goes to +∞ as t goes to 0. We let `(0) = +∞. By analogy to the correlation
     length studied in [Kes87], we call `(t) the sensitivity length, and it has the following
     interpretation (see Theorem 1.1): If n  `(t), then crossing events at scale n are
     not affected by a noise of intensity t. On the contrary, if n  `(t), a crossing event
     at scale n and its noised version behave roughly independently.
     Remark 1.3. At this point, the link between our definition of the sensitivity length
     (which is made by using only the four-arm probability) and the interpretation men-
     tioned above may not be clear. One of our main goals is actually to make this
     connection. More precisely: If n  `(t), then a first moment argument shows that
     no pivotal is affected by the noise and therefore one can indeed expect that con-
     nection properties do not change at scale n. On the contrary, if n  `(t), pivotal
     points start to be affected by the noise and therefore crossing events start to be af-
     fected themselves. The key difficulty is to show that they actually behave (almost)
     independently.


                                                     5
    The following theorem in the cases ? = 1 and ? = 1+ is a direct consequence
of [GPS10] (more generally, the proof from [GPS10] very likely extends to any
monochromatic arm event) but is new for the other arm types. The reason is that
spectral techniques have some limitations in the study of non-monotonic events (see
Open Problem 8 of [GPS10]).
Theorem 1.4. Let ? be any arm type and let ` be the sensitivity length defined in
(2) above. There exist c, C > 0 such that for every t ∈ [0, 1], we have
  1) (stability region) for every `(t) ≥ n ≥ m ≥ 1,
                                   ?      ?          ?
                                 cαm,n ≤ πm,n (t) ≤ αm,n ;

  2) (sensitivity region) for every n ≥ m ≥ `(t),
                                ?
                              (αm,n )2 ≤ πm,n
                                          ?            ?
                                              (t) ≤ C(αm,n )2 .

   Theorem 1.4 is proven in Section 7. In Section 8, we deduce Theorem 1.1 from
Theorem 1.4.

1.3    Exceptional times for dynamical percolation
In this section, we rely on the computation of the critical exponents for face percola-
tion on H from [LSW02, SW01], see Section 9. We refer to Section 10 for the study
of exceptional times for bond percolation on Z2 , for which these exponents are not
known. Let ω(0) be a critical percolation configuration on the hexagonal lattice, i.e.
                                                      ⊗H
                                             δ1 + δ0
                                ω(0) ∼
                                                2

(recall that H is the set of faces of the hexagonal lattice). We study the Markov
process t ∈ R+ 7→ ω(t) obtained by resampling the colours at rate 1. This process
was introduced in 1992 by Benjamini (unpublished) and independently in [HPS97].
It follows from known results on (static) percolation that for any fixed t, a.s. there
is no unbounded monochromatic component in ω(t). However, Schramm and Steif
[SS10] proved that there exist random times, called exceptional times, at which such
a property holds. Later, Garban, Pete and Schramm [GPS10] computed the exact
Hausdorff dimension of the set of exceptional times, and also proved the existence
of exceptional times for percolation on Z2 .
    We have the following theorem about the Hausdorff dimensions of exceptional
times. The upper bounds on these four dimensions have been computed in [SS10]
and the lower bound for Items 1 and 2 have been computed in [GPS10]. In Section 9,
we deduce the four lower bounds from Theorem 1.4. Let us note that it has been
proven in [GPS10] that the Hausdorff dimension from Item 3 is at least 1/9 and that
it was not known previously that the set of times from Item 4 was non-empty.
Theorem 1.5. The following holds a.s.:
 (1) the Hausforff dimension of the set of times with an unbounded black component
     is 31/36;
 (2) the Hausdorff dimension of the set of times with an unbounded black component
     in the upper half-plane is 5/9;


                                             6
 (3) the Hausforff dimension of the set of times with both a black and a white
     unbounded components is 2/3;
 (4) the Hausdorff dimension of the set of times with two disjoint infinite black
     paths and an unbounded white component is 1/9.
Remark 1.6. As proven in [SS10], a.s. there is no time with two disjoint unbounded
black components (which is equivalent to the fact that a.s. there is no time with
four infinite paths of alternating colors) and no time with both a black and a white
unbounded component in the half-plane. The following quantitative version of this
result is a consequence of [SS10] and Theorem 1.4. (More precisely, the upper
bounds are consequences of [SS10, Section 8] and one can prove the lower bounds
by using Theorem 1.4 and a second moment method analogous to that of the proof
of Theorem 1.5. We leave the details to the reader.) If j ≥ 4 and σ ∈ {0, 1}j is a
sequence which is not monochromatic, then
                                                         2
                   P [∃t ∈ [0, 1], fnσ (ω(t)) = 1] = n−(j −10)/12+o(1) .

If j ≥ 2 and σ ∈ {0, 1}j is a sequence which is not monochromatic, then
                                                    2
                P ∃t ∈ [0, 1], fnσ+ (ω(t)) = 1 = n−(2j +2j−9)/12+o(1) .

    In [HPS15], Hammond, Pete and Schramm have proven that an unbounded
component at a “uniformly chosen” exceptional time has the same law as the so-
called Incipient Infinite Cluster. The existence of exceptional times has also been
proven for percolation under (long range) exclusion dynamics, see [GV19], and for
Voronoi percolation in a dynamical environment, see [Van21]. The scaling limit of
dynamical percolation has been defined and studied in [GPS13, GPS18]. Dynamical
percolation has also been studied in a Liouville environment, see [GHSS21]. See
[Ros21] for the study of the scaling limit of dynamical Erdős–Renyi percolation.

1.4    Organization of the paper
The paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we present a sketch of proof of the
sharp noise sensitivity theorem and explain some connections with other works. In
Section 3, we prove a dynamical Margulis–Russo formula. In Section 4 we extract
a quasi-multiplicativity property for πm,n (t) from [GPS10, Section 5]. In Section 5,
we prove the differential inequalities that we will use in the next three sections. Our
main intermediate result is that the dynamical four-arm event has superquadratic
decay above the sensitivity length. This result is stated and proven in Section 6.
The sharp noise sensitivity results Theorems 1.1 and 1.4 are proven in Sections 7
and 8 respectively, and Theorem 1.5 is proven in Section 9. Finally, in Section 10,
we discuss consequences for bond percolation on Z2 .

Convention for the constants. In all the paper, c and C are positive con-
stants that are not necessarily the same at each occurrence. These constants are
independent of the scale parameters k, m, n, . . ., the time parameters s, t, u, . . ., the
coordinates i and the subsets of coordinates R, S, . . ., but may depend on the arm
type ?. Following this convention, we will often omit the quantifiers for the con-
stants. For example, the statement “∀t ψ(t) ≥ cϕ(t)” should be interpreted as


                                            7
“∃c > 0 ∀t ψ(t) ≥ cϕ(t)”. Occasionally, we may we need to fix a constant for
multiple uses, and we will make it clear by writing the constant with an index (e.g.
C1 , C2 , . . .). Finally, given two functions ϕ, ψ with non-negative values, we let

                                        ϕψ

if cϕ ≤ ψ ≤ Cϕ.

2     Discussion and sketch of proof
2.1    Sketch of proof
In this section, we present a sketch of proof of the sharp noise sensitivity results
Theorems 1.1 and 1.4. Recall that gn is the indicator of the left-right crossing of
[0, n]2 . In order to study the effect of the noise on the Boolean function gn , we
will use a dynamical version of Margulis–Russo’s formula (see Section 3) to show
          d
that − dt   Qt (gn )  n2 πn (t). This formula can be understood as the analogue for
noise sensitivity of the formula used to express the derivative in the parameter p of
crossing probabilities in terms of the four-arm probability. This implies the following
identity about the covariance of crossing events:
                                                         Z 1
                      COVt (gn ) = Qt (gn ) − Q1 (gn )      n2 πn (s)ds.           (3)
                                                        t

Equation (3) enables one to reduce the analysis of COVt (gn ) to that of πn (t), and
in the rest of this section we explain how to derive a precise expression of πn (t) up
to constants. To this purpose, we rely on an approach inspired by Kesten’s study of
the near-critical four-arm event [Kes87] (see also [Wer07, Nol08]). A key idea is to
apply again Margulis–Russo’s formula to the four-arm probability, which gives rise
to the following inequality for all n ≥ m ≥ 1 and t ∈ [0, 1]:
                                                    n
                                                    X
                              d
                       0≤−       log (πm,n (t)) ≤ C   kπk (t).                     (4)
                              dt
                                                   k=m

Remark 2.1. By (4), the quantities πm,n (t) are monotonic in t (even if the four-
arm event is not monotomic), which is a helpful property that has no analogue in
Kesten’s approach.

      defined in the domain D = [0, 1] × N∗ . This function is known at the boundary of
      the domain:
                              πn (0) = αn , πn (1) = αn2 , π1 (t) = 1,
      and we will use the PDI (together with other properties of this function) to compute
      it in the interior D.
          Recall that εn = n21αn and that `(t) is the sensitivity length defined in (2). In the

      exactly true, but justified by the fact that Smirnov and Werner [SW01] have proven
      that αn = n−5/4+o(1) for critical percolation on the hexagonal lattice.)

         Using the PDI (4) with m = 1, it follows from the definition of `(t) that πn (t) is

                                      ∀n ≤ `(t) πn (t)  αn = n−5/4 .                       (5)

      This step is exactly the same as in Kesten’s approach. The main difference is the
      study above the curve. Indeed, if p 6= pc , renormalization arguments imply that
      the percolation probabilities decay exponentially fast above the correlation length,
      while in the present context, we always stay at criticality and πn (t) will also decay
      polynomially fast above the sensitivity length.

The key step is to prove that the exponent β above the curve is strictly larger than

that this exponent β exists, this follows directly from
                                          (3)

Of course, the existence of β is a very strong assumption. However, in Section 6
(which is the key section of the paper), we will replace this assumption by the known
quasi-multiplicativity and monotonicity properties of πm,n (t), which together with
(6) will enable us to show that for all n ≥ m ≥ `(t),
                                 πn (t)     m 2+c

   By plugging (7) in the PDI (4), one can then show that the ratio πn (t)/πm (t) is
stable above the curve. Therefore,
                                              πn (t)   πn (1)  α2
                       ∀n ≥ m ≥ `(t)                         = 2n ,
                                              πm (t)   πm (1)  αm
which together with (5) concludes the desired computation of πn (t).
Remark 2.2. Our main intermediate result is (7): πn (t) is superquadratic above
the curve. Note that in near-critical percolation [Kes87], even the (black or white,
depending on if p < pc or p > pc ) one-arm event probability is superquadratic above
the curve since it is exponentially small. In order to prove (7), we rely on several
properties of πn (t), including properties that are not present in Kesten’s proof, such
as the monotonicity property (see Remark 2.1) and quasi-multiplicativity above the
curve.

2.2    Further connections with other works
A dynamical Margulis–Russo formula. The dynamical Margulis–Russo
formula used in the present paper (see Section 3) is not new. In particular, this
is a direct consequence of general covariance representations along Markov semi-
groups, see for instance [BGL13, Section 1.7.1 and Chapter 2]. Moreover, as ex-
plained in [GP20] where Galicza and Pete study sparse reconstruction of Boolean
functions, this is an analogue for Boolean functions of covariance formulas for the
Ornstein–Ulhenbeck dynamics, which are for instance central in Chatterjee’s theory
of superconcentration and chaos [Cha14] (see e.g. Section 4 of Chapter 2 from this
book). Analogous covariance formulas also play an important role in Pitterbarg’s
work [Pit96], which has been reinterpreted by using pivotal events (in a Gaussian
setting) in [RV19, BMR20].
    As explained in [BKS99, Section 5.4], COVt (gn ) can be seen as the variance
of the quenched probability of the crossing event on a random graph. From this


                                               10
       point view, the dynamical Margulis–Russo formula is very similar to Theorem 2.1
       of [AGMT16] that is used to study the quenched crossing probabilities in Voronoi
       percolation.

       Noise sensitivity via differential equations. In [EG20], Eldan and Gross
       study noise sensitivity (and other properties of Boolean functions) by using dif-
       ferential inequalities satisfied by COVt (f ). Contrary to the present paper, their
       techniques are based on stochastic calculus and they study Boolean functions in
       general.

       Upper and lower bounds on the pivotal probabilities. We refer to the
       beginning of Section 3 for the notion of pivotality and we recall (see for instance
       [Wer07]) that, if we neglect boundary issues, ∀i P[i is piv. for gn ]  αn . The
       classical result
                    P [BKS99, Theorem 1.3] states that the sequence gn is noise sensitive if
       and only if i P[i is piv. for gn ]2  n2 αn2 converges to 0 as n → ∞. And therefore,
       noise sensitivity follows from an upper bound on αn . On the contrary, one of the
       main inputs of our approach is the lower bound (1) on αn , which essentially means
       that there are many pivotals in expectation.

       Differential inequalities in percolation. As mentioned earlier, differential
       inequalities were used by Kesten to study the phase transition of percolation, but
       the interest of differential inequalities for percolation was also highlighted in several
       other works, see for instance [AB87] or the study of mean-field behavior [HH17].


       3     A dynamical Margulis–Russo formula
       In this section we prove a dynamical version of the Margulis–Russo formula, in
       the general framework of Boolean functions on the hypercube. Given a general
       Boolean function f : {0, 1}n → {0, 1}, we will express the derivative of Qt (f ) with
       respect to the noise parameter t in terms of the pivotal events. This formula will be
       instrumental in Section 5, where we will establish differential inequalities satisfied
       by the crossing and arm probabilities.
           We consider a heterogeneously noised configuration where the points are resam-
       pled with probability t inside a subset S ⊆ [n] := {1, · · · , n}, and fully resampled
       outside S.3 Let n ≥ 1, t ∈ [0, 1] and S ⊆ [n]. Also, let X = (X1 , · · · , Xn ) ∼ P and
       let Y = (Y1 , · · · , Yn ) ∼ P be obtained from X by resampling independently each co-
       ordinate i ∈ S with probability t and by resampling independently each coordinate
       i ∈ [n] \ S with probability 1. If f : {0, 1}n → {0, 1}, we let

                      QSt (f ) = E[f (X)f (Y )],   COVSt (f ) = Cov(f (X), f (Y )).
                        [n]                         [n]
       In particular, Qt (f ) = Qt (f ) and COVt (f ) = COVt (f ). If A ⊆ {0, 1}n , we let

                                           QSt (A) = QSt (1A ).
   3
     This will be useful later when studying the derivative of arm probabilities. The set S will be chosen
as the set of points away from the boundary of the considered domain, and it will allow us to ignore the
effect of points close the boundary for which the pivotality has a different interpretation than the point
in the “bulk”.


                                                    11
    It is known that if Y is a noised configuration of X, then the covariance between
f (X) and f (Y ) decreases when the noise increases (see [GS14, O’D14]). In the
present work, we will use the following monotonicity properties of QSt (f ) (that is
deduced below from general derivative formula with respect to the noise).
Proposition 3.1. Let f : {0, 1}n → {0, 1}. The quantity QSt (f ) is non-increasing
in t and non-decreasing in S.
    In order to state the main result of this section, let us recall the notion of piv-
otality associated to a Boolean function. Let n ≥ 1 and f : {0, 1}n → {0, 1}.
A coordinate i ∈ [n] is said to be pivotal for f in a configuration x ∈ {0, 1}n if
f (xi ) 6= f (x), where xi ∈ {0, 1}n is obtained from x by changing the ith coordinate.
Proposition 3.2 (Dynamical Margulis–Russo formula). Let f : {0, 1}n → {0, 1}
and S ⊆ [n]. For every t ∈ [0, 1], we have

                                d S          1X S
                        0≤−        Qt (f ) ≤   Qt (i is piv. for f ),
                                dt           4

and the second inequality is an equality when f is monotone.
Remark 3.3. More general versions of these propositions are known (for instance
when the measure is still product but not uniform), see e.g. [BGL13].
    In order to prove Proposition 3.2, we use the following coupling. Let S ⊂ [n].

     To prove that the right-hand side of (8) is non-negative, we introduce another
coupling of the law of (X, Y ) (where Y = Y (t1 , · · · , tn ) as above): We define si ∈
[0, 1] by 1 − ti = (1 − si )2 and we let X ∼ P. Moreover, we let W be obtained
from X by resampling independently each coordinate i ∈ S with probability si
and each coordinate i ∈ / S with probability 1. Furthermore, we let Y be obtained
from W by resampling independently each coordinate i ∈ S with probability si and
each coordinate i ∈ / S with probability 1. Then, (X, Y ) is a coupling of the law



                                                 13
of (X, Y ). Moreover, conditionally on W , X and Y are independent and have the
same distribution. Therefore,

is non-negative. (In other words, this non-negativity property comes from the re-
versibility of the dynamics.)

      6       Superquadratic decay above the sensitivity length
      In this section, we prove the following bound for the dynamical four-arm event,
      which is the central proposition of our paper. Recall that `(t) is the sensitivity
      length (defined in (2)).
      Proposition 6.1 (Superquadratic behaviour above the sensitivity length). There
      exist c, C > 0 such that, for every t ∈ [0, 1] and every n ≥ m ≥ `(t),

           The proof of the proposition above will involve only elementary analysis argu-

      been established in the previous sections. Before starting the proof, we gather the
      three main properties (P1-P3) that we will use.
           As mentioned earlier, our first main ingredient is the differential inequality sat-
      isfied by the dynamical four-arm probability from Lemma 5.3. By integrating this

Proof of Proposition 6.1. The proof is decomposed into three steps. First, we use
(P1) to show that the dynamical four-arm probability πn (t) behaves like αn under
the sensitivity length (i.e. for n ≤ `(t)), and then we use this estimate together with
(P2-P3) and the polynomial lower bound (20) to conclude the proof in two steps:
first a logarithmic, then the promised polynomial improvement.

9        Applications to dynamical percolation
9.1      Background on critical exponents
Let j ≥ 1 and let σ ∈ {0, 1}j be a sequence that is not monochromatic. Lawler,
Schramm and Werner [LSW02] and Smirnov and Werner [SW01] have proven that
                                                                            +
                           σ
                          αm,n = (m/n)ζj +o(1) ,          σ+
                                                         αm,n = (m/n)ζj +o(1) ,
where o(1) goes to 0 as m/n goes to 0 and where
 ζ1 = 5/48;        ζj = (j 2 − 1)/12 for every j ≥ 2;              ζj+ = (j 2 + j)/6 for every j ≥ 1.
Note that the Hausdorff dimensions from Theorem 1.5 are (2−ζ4 −ζ ? )/(2−ζ4 ), where
ζ ? equals ζ1 , ζ1+ , ζ2 and ζ3 respectively. Moreover, the exponents from Remark 1.6
are 2 − ζ4 − ζ ? .

9.2      Computation of the Hausdorff dimensions

proved in [SS10] (without using any spectral tool). We prove the lower bounds.

inequality and Frostman’s theorem, it is sufficient to show that, for every γ < 31/36
(resp. 5/9, 2/3 and 1/9) if ? = 1 (resp. 1+, 01 and 010), we have

10       Bond percolation on Z2
In this section, we consider bond percolation on the square lattice Z2 , which is
defined as follows: Each edge is independently open with probability p and closed
with probability 1 − p. Consider the dual lattice (Z2 )? and let each edge e? of this
dual lattice be open (resp. closed) if the unique edge e that intersects e? is closed
(resp. open). The primal open edges are colored in black and the dual open edges
are colored in white. The critical parameter of this model is pc = 1/2 [Kes80].
    In every proof except in Section 9 (where we prove Theorem 1.5 by using the
computation of the critical exponents for face percolation on the hexagonal lattice),
we have only used results that are also known for bond percolation on Z2 . In
particular, we have proven Theorems 1.1 and 1.4 for this model.
    Garban, Pete and Schramm have proven in [GPS10] that a.s. there exist excep-
tional times with an unbounded black component for percolation on Z2 . If one com-
bines their results with the bounds on the arm events probabilities from [DMT21],
one obtains that the Hausdorff dimension of such times is at least 3/4. By using
Theorem 1.4 and the bounds from [DMT21], we obtain a new proof of this result
and we also prove a lower bound on the Hausdorff dimension of exceptional times
with both a black and a white unbounded components.
Theorem 10.1. Consider critical dynamical bond percolation on Z2 . There exist
d1 ≥ 3/4 and d2 ≥ 1/2 such that a.s. the Hausdorff dimension of the set of times
with an unbounded black component equals d1 and the Hausdorff dimension of the
set of times with both a black and a white unbounded components equals d2 .

Proof. The fact that these Hausdorff dimensions are a.s. constant is a consequence
of Kolmogorov’s 0-1 law as explained in [SS10, Section 6]. Let ? = 1 or 01. As in
the proof of Theorem 1.5, it is sufficient to show that for any γ < 3/4 (resp. 1/2),
                                        Z 1
                               ? −1
                   sup ε1−γ
                        n   (α n )   +      t−γ (α`(t)
                                                  ?
                                                       )−1 dt < +∞.
                     n                  0

This is a direct consequence of the following estimates from [DMT21, Section 6.4]:

                   αn1 ≥ cn−1/6 ,   αn01 ≥ cn−1/3 ,   αn ≥ cn−4/3 .
